In addition to those disclosures generally permitted under 5 U.S.C. 552a(b) , all or a portion of the records or information contained in this system of records may be disclosed as a routine use pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 552a(b)(3) under the following circumstances. All disclosures made under these routine uses shall be limited to only those disclosures that may be made consistent with BJS's authorities, including 34 U.S.C. 10231(a) ; 34 U.S.C. 10134 ; and 28 CFR 22 . Accordingly, BJS will not disclose information for any purpose that is not a statistical or research purpose, and records will be disclosed only in accordance with BJS's confidentiality obligations. Sharing of records through these routine uses occurs only pursuant to written agreements and data use agreements that limit the recipients' use of the information to statistical or research purposes only, prohibit redisclosure except as authorized by BJS, and require appropriate technical and physical safeguards for the data.

A. To contractors, grantees, cooperative agreement recipients, experts, consultants, students, and others performing or working on a contract, service, grant, cooperative agreement, or other assignment for the Federal Government, when necessary to accomplish an agency function related to this system of records.

B. To such recipients and under such circumstances and procedures as are mandated by Federal statute or treaty.

C. To the news media and the public, including disclosures pursuant to 28 CFR 50.2 , unless it is determined that release of the specific information in the context of a particular case would constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.

D. To a Member of Congress or staff acting upon the Member's behalf when the Member or staff requests the information on behalf of, and at the request of, the individual who is the subject of the record.

E. To the National Archives and Records Administration for purposes of records management inspections conducted under the authority of 44 U.S.C. 2904 and 2906 .

F. To appropriate agencies, entities, and persons when (1) the Department suspects or has confirmed that there has been a breach of the system of records; (2) the Department has determined that as a result of the suspected or confirmed breach there is a risk of harm to individuals, the Department (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security; and (3) the disclosure made to such agencies, entities, and persons is reasonably necessary to assist in connection with the Department's efforts to respond to the suspected or confirmed breach or to prevent, minimize, or remedy such harm.

G. To another Federal agency or Federal entity, when the Department determines that information from this system of records is reasonably necessary to assist the recipient agency or entity in (1) responding to a suspected or confirmed breach or (2) preventing, minimizing, or remedying the risk of harm to individuals, the recipient agency or entity (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security, resulting from a suspected or confirmed breach.

H. To an actual or potential party to litigation or the party's authorized representative for the purpose of negotiation or discussion of such matters as settlement, plea bargaining, or in informal discovery proceedings.

I. To a former employee of the Department for purposes of (1) responding to an official inquiry by a Federal, State, or local government entity or professional licensing authority, in accordance with applicable Department regulations; or (2) facilitating communications with a former employee that may be necessary for personnel-related or other official purposes when the Department requires information or consultation assistance from the former employee regarding a matter within that person's former area of responsibility.

J. To Federal, State, local, Tribal, territorial, foreign, or international statistical and research agencies and entities for statistical and research purposes only, provided that the recipient agrees in writing to (1) use the information solely for statistical or research purposes; (2) maintain the confidentiality of the information consistent with the protections afforded under 34 U.S.C. 10231(a) and, where applicable, 34 U.S.C. 30303 ; (3) not redisclose the information except as authorized by BJS; and (4) implement appropriate administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the information from unauthorized access, use, or disclosure. Such disclosures may be made to support methodological research, data quality improvement, record linkage for statistical purposes, or the production of aggregate statistical products.

K. To any agency, organization, or individual for the purpose of performing audit or oversight operations as authorized by law, but only such information as is necessary and relevant to such audit or oversight function.

DISCLOSURE TO CONSUMER REPORTING AGENCIES:

None.

POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR STORAGE OF RECORDS:

Records in this system are stored electronically or on paper in secure

( printed page 65601)

facilities in a locked drawer behind a locked door. The records may be stored on magnetic disc, tape, digital media, and CD-ROM.

POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETRIEVAL OF RECORDS:

Records may be retrieved by any of the data elements listed in the “Categories of Records” section above. Although information is retrievable by personal identifiers, BJS retrieves records by personal identifiers only for statistical and research purposes, such as data linkage, quality control, or respondent follow-up, and not for administrative, enforcement, or determinations about individuals.

POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETENTION AND DISPOSAL OF RECORDS:

Records are retained and disposed of in accordance with DOJ and OJP records retention schedules as approved by the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA).

ADMINISTRATIVE, TECHNICAL, AND PHYSICAL SAFEGUARDS:

Records are maintained in a secure, password-protected electronic system that utilizes security hardware and software to include multiple firewalls, active intruder detection, and role-based access controls. Additionally, OJP's information technology systems have been accredited and certified in accordance with the Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) and DOJ security requirements. Access to the records in this system is restricted to those who require the records in the performance of their official duties and specifically those with statistical or research responsibilities. Access to the premises where the records are stored is restricted to authorized personnel and escorted visitors. BJS applies statistical disclosure limitation techniques to all data products prior to public release to prevent the identification of individual respondents or establishments.

RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURES:

All requests for access to records must be in writing and should be addressed to the Office of Justice Programs, Office of General Counsel, 810 Seventh Street NW, Washington, DC 20531. The envelope and letter should be clearly marked “Privacy Act Access Request.” The request must describe the records sought in sufficient detail to enable Department personnel to locate them with a reasonable amount of effort. The request must include a general description of the records sought and must include the requester's full name, current address, and date and place of birth. The request must be signed and either notarized or submitted under penalty of perjury.

Although no specific form is required, you may obtain forms for this purpose from the Director, Office of Privacy and Civil Liberties, United States Department of Justice, 145 N Street NE, Suite 8W.300, Washington, DC 20530, or on the Department of Justice website at
https://www.justice.gov/​privacy-page/​file/​Certification_​Identity.pdf/​download.

More information regarding the Department's procedures for accessing records in accordance with the Privacy Act can be found at 28 CFR part 16 subpart D, “Protection of Privacy and Access to Individual Records Under the Privacy Act of 1974.”

CONTESTING RECORD PROCEDURES:

Individuals seeking to contest or amend records maintained in this system of records must direct their requests to the address indicated in the “Record Access Procedures” paragraph, above. All requests to contest or amend records must be in writing and the envelope and letter should be clearly marked “Privacy Act Amendment Request.” All requests must state clearly and concisely what record is being contested, the reasons for contesting it, and the proposed amendment to the record. More information regarding the Department's procedures for amending or contesting records in accordance with the Privacy Act can be found at 28 CFR 16.46 , “Requests for Amendment or Correction of Records.”

NOTIFICATION PROCEDURES:

Individuals may be notified if a record in this system of records pertains to them when the individuals request information utilizing the same procedures as those identified in the “Record Access Procedures” paragraph, above.

EXEMPTIONS PROMULGATED FOR THE SYSTEM:

None.

The collections stem from the Commission's July 22, 2026 *Upper C-band Report and Order* (FCC 26-46), which requires incumbent Fixed Satellite Service operations to clear the 4.0-4.16 GHz band by December 30, 2030, or June 30, 2031, so that 160 megahertz (3.98-4.14 GHz) can be auctioned for flexible-use terrestrial wireless service by July 4, 2027, as mandated by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. It also establishes a Relocation Coordinator—selected by a committee of eligible space station operators, or procured by the Commission if no selection is made by January 1, 2027—to coordinate clearing schedules, perform engineering analyses, assign and track earth station migrations, review operators' Transition Plans, mediate disputes, and file quarterly reports. Eligible space station operators must additionally submit quarterly progress reports beginning March 31, 2027, timely Certifications of Completion, and notice of any transition delays within seven days; the first collection is estimated to involve 16,512 respondents, 34,871 responses, 123,465 annual burden hours, and $10,705,353 in annual costs, while the second involves 30 respondents and 30 responses.

summary_responses.response: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service has issued a final rule amending the Uniform Offering Circular (31 CFR part 356), which governs the sale and issuance of marketable book-entry Treasury bills, notes, and bonds, with an effective date of October 15, 2026. The amendments were prompted by Treasury's September 2026 announcement of a planned upgrade to its auction system, and they align the auction rules with that upgrade while making technical clarifications. Many changes are definitional or terminological—revising terms such as "adjusted value," "dated date," "index ratio," "issue date," "settlement amount," and "noncompetitive bid," removing outdated references (such as paper bids, the former CUSIP-issuing entity, and "inflation-indexed" securities), substituting "award" and "recognize" for "accept" and "tender," and replacing references to TreasuryDirect.gov with a general reference to Treasury's website—none of which alter how values for inflation-protected securities are calculated. The most substantive change requires submitters of noncompetitive customer bids to provide each individual customer's name and bid amount before the noncompetitive auction close, eliminating summary bid amounts so that Treasury staff can complete post-auction operations earlier in the day. Treasury determined the rule is not significant under Executive Order 12866 and is exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act's notice-and-comment and delayed effective date requirements because Treasury securities are contracts, and it likewise found the Regulatory Flexibility Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, and major-rule provisions of the Congressional Review Act inapplicable.

VIII Conclusions

In this paper, we have examined retries as a mechanism for prioritizing transactions in cloud microservice architectures and for mitigating orchestrated overload situations. Our proposed mechanism, DiffTry (Differential Retries), is based on a simple and lightweight distributed and stateless implementation, requiring no coordination or state sharing between microservices.

Our analysis derived the per-class rejection probabilities and throughput in a single-service system, and then extended these results to general microservices networks. The analysis provides practitioners with a quantitative framework for selecting retry limits, together with monotonicity guarantees ensuring that increasing the retry limit of a class increases its end-to-end success rate.
Further, we have validated our analysis using both simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment in which DiffTry was implemented as a simple extension of Istio's retry policies.

Our results show that DiffTry provides substantial protection to high-priority transactions, often reducing their rejection rates by factors of several times, while remaining dormant under normal (no-overload) conditions and requiring no application-level changes.

Future work may consider the integration of DiffTry with complementary overload-control mechanisms, such as centralized admission control and auto-scaling policies, to further improve resilience under adversarial or highly dynamic workloads.

claim_breakdown.claim: DiffTry is implemented as part of standard retry logic without requiring changes to service code, orchestration, or runtime infrastructure.
DiffTry incurs no computational or memory cost beyond standard retry logic.
DiffTry handles each request independently without maintaining per-request state or history.
DiffTry operates without overload detection and remains dormant with minimal effect under normal load conditions.
In the DiffTry model, requests are divided into at least two priority classes, where each class is assigned a specific retry limit.
The analytical model assumes that the transaction rejection probability is independent across different retry attempts.
Under extreme service time variability (modeled as a hyper-exponential distribution), the independence assumption can be relaxed while yielding the same transaction rejection probabilities.
For single-service systems, the fluid model for overload and the M/M/1/m queueing model for no-overload both yield a unique solution for the transaction rejection probability.

In single-service simulations with an arrival rate 2.5 times the server capacity, assigning 5 retries to class 1 and 0 to class 2 resulted in a 15% rejection probability for class 1 versus 73% for class 2.

For general networks with a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) topology, the network traffic equations can be solved sequentially to find a unique solution for rejection probabilities and transaction rates.
For cyclic networks, an iterative algorithm is proposed that is proven to converge monotonically to a solution for the network equations.

Numerical studies on a 10-node overloaded network demonstrated that increasing the retry limit of the high-priority class monotonically increases both its completion rate and the overall system completion probability.
DiffTry was experimentally evaluated on a Kubernetes cluster with 10 microservices using the Istio service mesh to enforce class-based retry policies.
In the Kubernetes evaluation, increasing the high-priority retry limit significantly reduced high-priority rejection rates while only mildly increasing latency and overall resource consumption.

key_fact_breakdown.key_fact: DiffTry (Differential Retries) is a stateless mechanism that assigns different retry-attempt limits to different priority classes of requests to achieve differentiation in rejection rates.
Under overload with DiffTry, high-priority requests achieve a rejection rate of around 15% and account for about 85% of successful completions when both classes contribute 50% of input load.
DiffTry requires neither overload sensing nor microservices coordination and is implemented as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application code changes.

The paper develops an analytical model for DiffTry starting with two services in tandem, then generalizes it to networks of services using an open-network model combined with flow classes and priorities.

The paper proves that network-wide class-level success rates increase monotonically with retry limits and validates the analysis on a live Kubernetes deployment where measured rejection closely matches the theoretical predictions.
DiffTry assigns different retry attempt limits to requests from different priority classes to prioritize high-value transactions during overload.

summary_responses.response: The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to its Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations in 5 CFR part 630, subpart L, to incorporate statutory amendments enacted in January 2021 (Public Law 116-283) and December 2023 (Public Law 118-31), with an effective date of December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026. The 2021 amendments broadened eligibility by making virtually all civilian Federal service—including temporary, intermittent, Postal Service, Postal Regulatory Commission, and non-appropriated fund instrumentality service—count toward the 12-month qualifying service requirement, while still requiring employees to meet the statutory definition of a covered "employee" to actually use title 5 FMLA leave. Those amendments also clarified that annual and sick leave earned under authorities outside title 5 may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, and excluded all Veterans Health Administration employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage, as they are instead governed by 38 U.S.C. 7425(c). The 2023 amendment further expanded eligibility by allowing honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps—but not the Coast Guard or the Public Health Service commissioned corps—to count toward the 12-month service requirement, so employees may combine qualifying civilian and military service. Because paid parental leave (PPL) is substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, these changes also affect PPL eligibility; the rule simply codifies clear statutory requirements and prior OPM guidance issued in memoranda CPM 2021-07 and CPM 2024-05.
